newsitem.title: USA: Feinstein may be aiming for California governor.
newsitem.headline: Feinstein may be aiming for California governor.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, Political Correspondent
Dianne Feinstein, the Democratic Senator from California, wants Americans to know she is tough on crime. Very tough.

It is an important message, especially for her constituents in California, because Feinstein may try again for governor of the nation's most populous state in 1998. If she won, she would be at or near the top of most lists for Democratic vice presidential nominee two years later.
Feinstein made the Democratic short list once before in 1984, but presidential nominee Walter Mondale decided to pick another woman -- Representative Geraldine Ferraro of New York.

Asked in a Reuters interview whether she would run for governor, Feinstein was cagey but ruled nothing out. "I don't feel a need to make a decision at this stage. I've run statewide now three times. I have a substantial base. If I decide to go, I'll go," she said.

She then provided a detailed analysis of her electoral position, noting her huge strength in her home base around San Francisco Bay and her growing strength in Los Angeles County. Add to that her appeal as a female candidate.
"Women clearly elected this president (Clinton). I think women are coming alive as a very vocal majority," she said.
California may be more hospitable to Democrats than in the recent past, Feinstein said, especially as the fast-growing Hispanic population begins to assert itself at the polls.
"The pendulum swings and it's been 16 years since there's been a Democratic governor. So there is a very good opportunity," she said.
The likely Republican nominee is Attorney General Dan Lungren, a strong law-and-order man. So burnishing her anti-crime credentials makes good sense for Feinstein.

In 1994, she was a key figure in the passage of legislation banning the manufacture, sale and possession of military-style assault weapons. This year she is backing legislation to combat the growing problem of gang violence, an issue Feinstein feels strongly about.
"I believe that street gangs have become much more of a threat to the American way of life than organised mafia-type inspired crime has ever been," she said.

The bill would double criminal penalties for gang members who commit federal crimes, apply racketeering statutes to gang crimes and make recruitment of minors into gangs a federal offence with stiff penalties.
At the same time Feinstein is leading efforts to recruit Democrats for an amendment to the U.S. Constitution to guarantee special rights for crime victims.

At 63 Feinstein is a veteran of some of the toughest election battles the country has seen in recent years. A former popular two-term mayor of San Francisco, she narrowly lost to Pete Wilson in her first run for governor in 1990 but rebounded in 1992 to win election to the Senate.

Two years later, she found herself in a venomous race against Republican millionaire Michael Huffington, who spent more than $30 million, much of it on negative TV ads, in an effort to unseat her. Feinstein won, but only just.
Now, some of her would-be Democratic rivals for the governor's job are warning her not to run again so soon.

Lt. Gov. Gray Davis told the Los Angeles Times last week that Feinstein should "forget about it." He added, "She's not what she used to be. She has taken too many blows in too many brawls. She's walking wounded."

Feinstein dismissed Gray's comments as "misplaced bravado" and said she had repaired any damage inflicted by past fights. Asked if she was tired of running for office after three hard campaigns in the past six years, she said, "It takes a short-term toll. I don't think it takes a long-term toll."
Those are not the words of a woman scared of yet another campaign.
